name: Murik / Ngorek
confidence_why: Smith 2017, from fieldwork with Ngorek speakers at Long Semiang, describes weak penultimate stress, but Blust's 1971 field notes from the same village mark final stress on every citation form; Blust 2013 observes that many Sarawak languages have final stress in citation forms and penultimate stress in phrases, which would reconcile the two, though no source settles it for Murik itself.
catalog_citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. The Languages of Borneo: A Comprehensive Classification. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa (Robert Blust, chair). 724 pp. Section 2.2.2 'Murik-Merap'.
catalog_locator: pp. 62-63, sec. 2.2.2 Murik-Merap; file (pp. 92-93); open copy via the Internet Archive of ling.hawaii.edu
catalog_quote: Murik-Merap contain two distinct groups of languages, the Murik group which consists of Murik/Ngorek4, Pua’, and Huang Bau (Soriente 2003), and the Merap language, which is spoken in the Malinau area of North Kalimantan. Synchronically, Merap and Murik could not be more different. Merap has strong word-final stress, 26 vowels including diphthongs, triphthongs, length, and nasality distinctions, while Murik is a conservative language, even by Kayanic standards, and has weak penultimate stress with a standard six vowel inventory of i, e, a, o, u, and ə. [fn. 4: Murik and Ngorek both appear in the literature in reference to the same language. Because the speakers I worked with at Long Semiang preferred to be called “Ngorek” I will use that term to refer to the specific dialect of Murik-Merap spoken at Long Semiang, and Murik to refer to the larger group, which contains Pua’ and Huang Bau.]
world_status: statement found in an open source

May 2017, By Alexander D. Smith, Dissertation Committee: Robert Blust, Chairperson'). extracted text of PDF pages 92-93 = printed pp. 62-63, section '2.2.2 Murik-Merap'. The quoted passage is there verbatim, running across the p. 62/63 page break: 'Synchronically, Merap and Murik could not be more different. Merap has strong word-final stress, 26 vowels including diphthongs, triphthongs, | length, and nasality distinctions, while Murik is a conservative language, even by Kayanic standards, and has weak penultimate stress with a standard six vowel inventor…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Murik proper (Ngorek of Long Semiang, Baram, Sarawak) has weak, non-contrastive stress on the penultimate syllable; the Merap dialect (Langap, Malinau, N. Kalimantan) has shifted to strong, invariant final stress (Smith 2017 OL 56:158: 'In Merap, stress appears regularly on the final syllable').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Murik/Ngorek. For Merap: 'words with CVCCVC structures receive a secondary stress in Merap: ˌCVCˈCVC' (Smith 2017 OL 56:159; dissertation p. 72).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Murik. For Merap: no stressed schwa; historical final-syllable schwa took stress and lowered to a (halaŋ [haˈlaŋ]); vowel clusters like kiawə̯ stressed [kiˈawə̯].
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation-form elicitation (Smith's own fieldwork at Long Semiang, 2014-2018). The Murik statement is a one-sentence characterisation in a subgrouping chapter, not a full phonology section; Blust 2013 notes generally that Borneo stress is non-phonemic and that some interior Sarawak languages show final stress only in citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog muri1259 'Murik (Malaysia)' [mxr] covers Murik proper = Ngorek of Long Semiang (Baram, Sarawak; Smith's consultants prefer 'Ngorek', fn. 4 p. 62 and OL fn. 11 p. 162) and, as a dialect, Merap (mera1243; Langap, Malinau, N. Kalimantan). The two differ sharply in stress: Murik/Ngorek weak penultimate (the quoted statement), Merap strong invariant final stress with secondary stress on CVC initial syllables (Smith 2017 OL 56(1):158-159; dissertation pp. 68, 72). Kalimantan Murik varieties Pua' and Huang Bau (Soriente 2003) are not described for stress in any opened source. The earlier scan classification no source found is superseded.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records penultimate stress (stress on syllable 2 of 2, 2 of 3, 3 of 4) on the strength of Smith 2017:62-63 ('Murik.. has weak penultimate stress'). Blust's 1971 transcriptions of the same variety (Long Semiang; Smith's Ngorek consultant Peter Ding Tingang was also at Long Semiang, Smith 2017 p. 62 fn. 4 and language list) consistently mark final stress in citation forms. Blust 2013:186 (ch. 4) offers the likely reconciliation without naming Murik: 'many of the languages of coastal Sarawak, and some interior languages have final stress in citation forms, but penultimate stress in phrasal context'.
new_statements.translation_language: Handwritten phonetic transcription with English glosses
new_statements.rule_in_words: The notebook contains no sentence about stress, but Blust's stress mark (an apostrophe placed before the stressed syllable, as calibrated on his Narum forms, e.g. tum'baŋ = Blust 2013:242 [tumbáŋ] 'stress is final', and on his Bimanese forms 'voʔo, sa'ŋufi = penultimate) is placed before the last syllable in every stress-marked Murik citation form, disyllables and trisyllables alike (ta'lɔʔ, li'maʔ, pi'tan, pu'lu, kəla'toŋ, təna'ʔin, palu'lup, ŋabu'yan, bali'rən, kəla'wéəŋ, bəla'téək). So the 1971 Long Semiang citation forms show word-final stress. Many forms (luaʔ, tusu, sayaʔ, ənəm, and most of the running vocabulary on pp. 144-145) carry no mark at all; no marked form has non-final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None marked. One note on emphasis: '87. bə'toŋ (but [ɓəə'toŋ] when emphasized)' (p. 141), i.e. lengthening of the pretonic vowel under emphasis, stress still final. Sentence data on p. 145 carry no stress marks.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Unmarked forms are simply unmarked, not marked elsewhere; '(tu.mpit)' on p. 139 marks a syllable boundary in tumpit 'heel', not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both the notebook and Smith 2017 describe the Murik of Long Semiang (upper Baram, Sarawak), which Smith's consultants call Ngorek; Smith uses 'Murik' for the wider group (Pua', Huang Bau). Blust notes a second Murik longhouse, Long Banyok. The catalog's 'Murik / Ngorek' entry matches this variety. Blust 1974 'A Murik vocabulary' (SMJ 22) is the published product of these notes and is not open online; Smith 2017 separately reports strong word-final stress for Merap (mera1243), a different language.

readall_conflicts: Blust's 1971 Long Semiang field notes (RB2-003-A pp. 139-146) mark stress on the final syllable of every stress-marked citation form (ta'lɔʔ '3', li'maʔ '5', pi'tan '9', pu'lu '10', kəla'toŋ 'people', təna'ʔin 'intestines', palu'lup 'thoughts', ŋabu'yan, bali'rən, kəla'wéəŋ), with the apostrophe-before-stressed-syllable convention confirmed on his Narum (tum'baŋ = Blust 2013:242 [tumbáŋ], 'stress is final') and Bimanese ('voʔo, sa'ŋufi, penultimate) pages of the same notebook. Smith 2017:62-63, describing the same village's dialect (Ngorek of Long Semiang), says Murik 'has weak penultimate stress'. The two sources therefore disagree on the same variety, 43 years apart. Blust 2013:186 states that many Sarawak languages have final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress in phrasal context, which would make both observations true of different speech styles; Blust's sentence data on p. 145 are unmarked, so the notebook itself cannot decide this. No source states that stress is contrastive; Smith calls it weak.
